questions.q: How does the chapter compare vector distance syntax between SQL Server 2025 and Oracle 23ai?
options: SQL Server 2025: VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', a, b); Oracle 23ai: VECTOR_DISTANCE(a, b, COSINE) - both chose function-based syntax the chapter expects a future SQL standard to converge on
SQL Server uses an operator <#> while Oracle uses a function
Both use identical syntax: VECTOR_DISTANCE(a, b, 'cosine')
SQL Server 2025 has no distance function; Oracle 23ai does
questions.explain: The chapter's comparison table shows SQL Server 2025 VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', a, b) vs Oracle 23ai VECTOR_DISTANCE(a, b, COSINE), noting the function-based syntax both vendors chose is easier to standardize than operator overloading.

questions.q: In the chapter's T-SQL reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) example, what is the RRF constant and why is RRF robust?
options: k = 10; it only works on pre-normalized scores
k = 60.0; RRF fuses ranks rather than distances, so it needs no score normalization and is robust when the two lists use incomparable scales
k = 1000; it averages the two ranked lists
k = 0.7; it weights semantic results more heavily
questions.explain: The T-SQL example uses DECLARE @k FLOAT = 60.0 and computes 1.0/(@k + rank) per list. RRF fuses ranks, not distances, so it needs no score normalization and works when semantic distances and full-text ranks are on incomparable scales.

questions.q: In the chapter's hybrid query combining semantic similarity with full-text rank, what weighting is used as the starting point?
options: 0.5 / 0.5 equal weighting
0.3 semantic + 0.7 full-text
0.7 semantic + 0.3 full-text rank, tuned against offline evaluation datasets
1.0 semantic only; full-text is display-only
questions.explain: The hybrid ORDER BY uses (0.7 * (1 - VECTOR_DISTANCE(...))) + (0.3 * (fts.[RANK] / 1000.0)); the chapter calls 0.7/0.3 a starting point to be tuned against offline evaluation datasets (Chapter 27).

questions.q: According to the chapter, in which workloads do dedicated vector databases still beat in-engine SQL Server vector indexes?
options: Small datasets under 10K vectors
Queries with only structured predicates
Workloads that need transactional consistency
>500M vectors in a single namespace (native graph sharding), thousands-of-tenant namespace isolation, sparse+dense hybrid search, and sub-10ms p99 at massive scale
questions.explain: The chapter's 'where dedicated wins' table lists: >500M vectors single namespace, Pinecone-style namespace multi-tenancy, native sparse+dense hybrid (SPLADE), and sub-10ms p99 at massive scale - gaps it calls engineering problems, not fundamental limitations.

questions.q: How does the chapter implement ColBERT-style multi-vector retrieval in SQL Server today?
options: With a dedicated MULTIVECTOR column type
With a child table ChunkTokenVectors holding one VECTOR(128) per token, a DiskANN index on it, and a MaxSim-approximation query taking MIN cosine distance per chunk grouped by ChunkId
It cannot be done in SQL Server at all
By storing all token vectors in a single VECTOR(MAX) column
questions.explain: The pattern is a child table dbo.ChunkTokenVectors (TokenVector VECTOR(128) per token, DiskANN index) with a query computing MIN(VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', TokenVector, @qt)) per ChunkId - the single-token building block of MaxSim, aggregated per query token in the application layer.
